malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Custom install commands are used for legitimate post-install tasks, but not for hidden or unauthorized code execution.
key_indicators: Custom install command registration in setup.py
Potential for hidden code execution via cmdclass

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains multiple instances of malicious code in setup.py and other files that exfiltrate installation and system events to attacker-controlled endpoints, download and execute remote payloads, and disguise malicious activity using evasion techniques. These behaviors enable unauthorized data exfiltration, arbitrary code execution, and potential for further compromise, all without user consent.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code in setup.py, post_install.py, or __init__.py is triggered during installation or import, initiating the attack sequence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of payloads or exfiltration of system/user data.

attack_chain.action: Payloads are downloaded, decoded, or executed, or system information is collected for exfiltration.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of data or further code execution on the victim system.

attack_chain.action: Data is exfiltrated to attacker-controlled endpoints (such as Discord webhooks or oastify.com), or further malicious actions are performed using executed payloads.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives installation events or system/user data, enabling further attacks or persistent access.

behavioral_signatures: Network requests in setup.py, post_install.py, or __init__.py during installation or import
Dynamic code execution via exec of remote or base64-decoded payloads
Base64 decoding and execution of files disguised as images (e.g., .png)
Custom install command hijacking in setup.py to trigger hidden code execution
File drop and execution of new Python scripts during installation
file_indicators: setup.py containing network requests or exec statements
post_install.py or __init__.py with exfiltration or payload execution logic
Files with image extensions (e.g., .png) containing base64-encoded payloads
Presence of dropped files such as malicious.py created during installation
network_indicators: Connections to Discord webhooks (discord.com/api/webhooks/...)
Connections to oastify.com, burpcollaborator.net, pipedream.net, oast.fun
Connections to thirdparty.site, paste.fo, transfer.sh, cdn.discordapp.com, dl.dropbox.com, mediafire.com, rentry.co, raw.githubusercontent.com, render.com
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for network requests or exec statements in setup.py, __init__.py, or post_install.py during installation or import. Flag packages that download and execute remote code, especially if using base64 decoding or disguising payloads as images. Alert on connections to known exfiltration or payload hosting domains during installation or import. Detect custom install command hijacking that triggers hidden code execution. Look for dropped files (e.g., malicious.py) and image files containing base64-encoded payloads.

matched_knowledge.source_package: bananasquad, kekwltd, and related packages (multiple, similar structure) (PyPI)

matched_snippet.code_behavior: During installation, the code spawns a hidden subprocess to silently install additional dependencies from PyPI, ensuring the malicious environment is set up without user awareness.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Silently installing dependencies via a hidden subprocess is a common tactic to conceal malicious activity and evade user scrutiny.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages declare dependencies in requirements.txt or setup.py, not by executing hidden subprocesses during installation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some installers may suppress windows for user experience, but not for dependency installation or to hide malicious actions.
key_indicators: subprocess creation with CREATE_NO_WINDOW flag
hidden installation of dependencies outside standard packaging mechanisms

They are distributed in large numbers under various names, all containing similar malicious payloads targeting Windows users, and employ advanced anti-analysis and persistence techniques.

attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and evasion of security tools.

attack_chain.action: Hide malicious files, self-delete, and capture screenshots and webcam images.

behavioral_signatures: Creation of hidden subprocesses for dependency installation during package setup
Environment checks for virtual machines, sandboxes, or test users followed by self-termination
Extraction of browser credentials, cookies, and payment data
Monitoring and replacement of clipboard contents matching cryptocurrency address patterns
Modification or replacement of app.asar files in Exodus or other Electron-based applications
Fetching and execution of remote, obfuscated payloads from attacker-controlled domains
Execution of PowerShell commands to disable Windows Defender and modification of the hosts file to block security domains
Hiding of created files and self-deletion of package scripts and executables
Unauthorized screen and webcam capture routines
Injection of JavaScript into Discord application files and forced process termination
Creation of password-protected zip archives containing user data and exfiltration via multiple channels
file_indicators: Randomly named .pyw files in temporary or user directories
Modified app.asar files in Exodus or other Electron app directories
Hidden files or directories created by the package in user or temp locations
Password-protected zip archives containing user data in user directories
network_indicators: Outbound connections to bananasquad[.]ru, kekwltd[.]ru, transfer[.]sh, gofile.io, anonfiles.com
Use of Discord webhook URLs (e.g., discord[.]com/api/webhooks/...) for data exfiltration
Telegram bot API traffic for fallback exfiltration
Unusual outbound traffic to public file-sharing services from Python processes
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Python packages that spawn hidden subprocesses during installation, perform environment checks to evade VMs or sandboxes, or access browser and application data. Detect clipboard access patterns that match cryptocurrency addresses and replacement with known attacker-controlled addresses. Watch for unauthorized modifications to third-party application files (such as app.asar in Exodus), creation of randomly named .pyw files, and password-protected zip archives in user directories. Network monitoring should flag connections to known malicious domains, Discord webhooks, and Telegram bot APIs, as well as unexpected uploads to file-sharing services. Endpoint security should alert on PowerShell commands disabling Defender, hosts file modifications targeting security domains, and attempts to hide or delete package files post-installation. Correlate these behaviors to identify coordinated malicious activity.
